title: Under Pontius Pilate (CCC 595–598)
hook: the Church teaches that Jews are not collectively responsible for his death; all sinners share it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hidden life: the carpenter of Nazareth, subject to Mary and Joseph. Your line was nazareth counts. Which plain job did you do slowly and well? Day one thousand seventy-six.

In the middle of the Creed, between the words about God and the words about eternity, there's a Roman official. Suffered under Pontius Pilate. A provincial governor, named in a profession of faith. Some readers hear his name as a pin in a map: this happened in a real place, under a real government, at a real time. But his name raises a harder question too, one the Catechism doesn't dodge. Who is responsible for the death of Jesus? Christians have given terrible answers to that question, and the Catechism says so. Today's word is the Creed's own phrase.
screen: `A ROMAN OFFICIAL IN THE CREED.` → `A PIN IN A MAP.` → `WHO IS RESPONSIBLE?`

segments.voice: Start with the Gospels themselves. They tell a tangled story: a betrayal by a friend, some of the religious authorities in Jerusalem, a crowd stirred up in the moment, and a governor who finds no cause, washes his hands, and hands Jesus over anyway. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment, and Rome carried it out. The Catechism says the trial's history is complex, and that the personal guilt of each person involved is known to God alone. Then it says something with real weight. The responsibility cannot be laid on the Jews of Jerusalem as a whole, let alone on Jewish people in other places and later times. It quotes the Second Vatican Council: what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, without distinction, nor against the Jews of today. And Jews are not to be spoken of as rejected or accursed, as if scripture taught it. Then the Catechism turns the question around. It quotes an older catechism, the Roman one: sinners were the authors and ministers of all the sufferings Christ endured. All sinners. Which means, it says, that Christians themselves carry the gravest share, and it admits that Christians have all too often laid that burden on the Jews alone. It's a confession, written into a book of teaching. And at the center of it is the man on the cross, who in Luke's Gospel prays for the people killing him. In the Douay-Rheims: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." So the Creed's phrase keeps two things together. A real governor, in a real province. And a death that, in Catholic teaching, belongs to no single people, because every sinner has a hand in it.
screen: `A TANGLED STORY, A ROMAN CROSS.` · `NOT THE JEWS AS A WHOLE.` · `SINNERS WERE THE AUTHORS.` · `CHRISTIANS CARRY THE GRAVEST SHARE.` · then, large: `FATHER, FORGIVE THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reject one prejudice. Settle, and breathe. Let a group of people come to mind that you sometimes lump together: by religion, by country, by politics, by the neighborhood they're from. Notice the shortcut sentence that comes with them, the one that starts with they all. Don't argue with it yet. Just see it. Then bring to mind one real person from that group, with a face and a name if you can. Let the shortcut sit next to the person, and see which one is truer. If you pray, you can use the words from the cross: Father, forgive them. The bell holds the time.
Under Pontius Pilate. The Creed's anchor in history, and the Catechism's reminder that the Passion is charged to no single people: all sinners share it. Today's word.
Your line: we all share it. Today, when you hear a sentence that starts with they all, about any group, notice it, and let it go unrepeated. Day one thousand seventy-six.

howItsDone: Catholics profess "suffered under Pontius Pilate" in the Creed, and Catholic teaching, following the Second Vatican Council, rejects blaming the Jewish people for the death of Jesus.
